[src/Particles.jl] function allocate_buffers(::AdamsBashforth{K}, tracers::Tracers) where {K}
[src/Particles.jl] mutable struct MultistepBuffers{V, S}  past / steps / filled
[src/phenomenology/Spectra.jl] struct ModelSpectrum{...}  C_K; large_scale; dissipation; ref::Reference
[src/phenomenology/Spectra.jl] provenance(m::ModelSpectrum) = m.ref
[src/Generator.jl] function FlowConditions(; viscosity, schmidt, ...)   # unchecked
findings.after:
# NO `::AbstractIntegrator` FALLBACK ...  [the 0.3 method is deleted]
[src/Particles.jl] function allocate_buffers(::AdamsBashforth{K}, tracers::Tracers, cache) where {K}
[src/Particles.jl] struct MultistepBuffers{C, S}  cache / startup / weights / nodes
[src/phenomenology/Spectra.jl] struct ModelSpectrum{...}  C_K; large_scale; dissipation
[src/phenomenology/Spectra.jl] _reference(::LargeScaleFactor, ::DissipationFactor) =
  throw(ArgumentError("this combination ... is not a published model, so it has no reference"))
[src/Generator.jl] viscosity > 0 || throw(ArgumentError(...));  schmidt > 0 || throw(ArgumentError(...))
findings.why_it_matters: Five removals of previously working usage, none announced. (1) Deleting `_base_cfl(::AbstractIntegrator)` means a user-defined `AbstractIntegrator` subtype — the documented extension point — now MethodErrors inside `recommended_cfl`, which is the default value of `Simulation`'s `cfl` keyword, so constructing a Simulation with a custom scheme fails where it previously ran at 0.3. (2) The 2-argument `allocate_buffers(AdamsBashforth(), tracers)` method is gone from an exported generic, and `MultistepBuffers`' documented fields `past`, `steps`, `filled` no longer exist, so any code reading the multistep history breaks. (3) `AdamsBashforth(order = 9)` and above now throws; the quadratic argument is correct, but orders 9+ previously constructed and ran. (4) `ModelSpectrum`'s plain constructor lost an argument and `provenance` went from returning a stored `Reference` to throwing for any pairing outside the three presets, so a user-composed model that reported its own provenance now errors. (5) `FlowConditions(viscosity = 0, ...)` is refused, which removes the inviscid (Euler / Re = ∞) configuration that the integrating factor handles exactly as the identity. Each guard has a real motivation in its comment; collectively they narrow the accepted input set well past the defects named, and none of them is a defect the diff demonstrates a run hitting.

findings.title: Empty-band guard regressed from a relative, divisor-safe test back to bare positivity, reopening a near-zero-denominator blow-up
findings.before: (base 569e6fc) `band_value < 1e-12 && return field   # nothing in the band yet (guard)` — an intermediate commit (f557311) then made this `_band_is_empty(band_value, total_value) = band_value <= eps(typeof(band_value)) * total_value || band_value <= 1e-12 * total_value || !(band_value > zero(band_value))`, explicitly to catch a band that is negligible RELATIVE to the field's total energy before dividing by it
findings.after: `_band_is_empty(band_value) = !(isfinite(band_value) && band_value > zero(band_value))`, used at `apply_forcing!`: `_band_is_empty(band_value) && return field` and at `set_forcing_rate!`: `amplitude = _band_is_empty(band_observable) ? 0.0 : forcing.injection_rate / (2 * band_observable)`
findings.why_it_matters: `apply_forcing!(::BandRescaling,...)` computes `scale = sqrt(target_band / band_value)` and applies `scale - 1` as an in-band amplification factor; `set_forcing_rate!(::ConstantPower,...)` divides `injection_rate` by `2*band_observable`. Any band_value that is tiny-but-positive (round-off in a low-wavenumber shell that has genuinely little energy, or Float32 underflow) now passes the guard and produces an arbitrarily large multiplier/amplitude in a single step — exactly the divide-by-near-zero blow-up the intermediate relative guard existed to prevent. The commit that removed it (ea57297) justifies the removal only by "multiplying by s² cannot change a sign, so the sign alone already has the invariance" — true for the on/off decision's scale-invariance, but that argument says nothing about the magnitude of 1/band_value when band_value is minuscule but positive; it discards the divisor-safety property along with the extra `inner` reduction it was paying for. No test in the suite (including the newly added r5-test-critic-06, which only exercises the exact-zero / negative-clamped cases) exercises a tiny-but-positive band_value, so this regression is currently untested.

findings.title: The CFL ceiling silently caps Δt below the true advective limit for any run with characteristic speed below 1 (in code units), not just the pathological round-off floor it targets
findings.before: `return speed > 0 ? sim.cfl * Δx / speed : sim.cfl * Δx` (the zero-speed branch only, an edge case reached solely when the flow is exactly at rest)
findings.after: `ceiling = sim.cfl * Δx` `return speed > 0 ? min(sim.cfl * Δx / speed, ceiling) : ceiling`
findings.why_it_matters: `min(cfl·Δx/speed, cfl·Δx)` picks the ceiling whenever `speed < 1` — a threshold set purely by the arithmetic, with no basis in the run's actual velocity scale, domain size, or viscosity (the ceiling is dimensionally `cfl·Δx`, i.e. it implicitly assumes a characteristic velocity of exactly 1 in whatever units the run happens to use). The stated defect (an unforced run's speed decaying to the ~2e-16 round-off floor, sending Δt to ~1e15) only requires guarding against speed approaching that floor; instead the fix binds for the entire regime `speed < 1`, which for the package's own default (`kinetic_energy = 1.5`, giving rms speed ≈ 1) is reached partway through any ordinary decaying-turbulence run, or immediately for any user who requests a lower `kinetic_energy`. In that regime the code now silently takes a smaller Δt than the CFL condition actually permits, altering the timestep sequence (and hence the exact numerical trajectory and step count) for previously well-posed, non-pathological inputs — not merely defusing the reported runaway.

findings.title: max_wavenumber/_build_dealias unification propagates a premature Float32 rounding of the exact rational cutoff fraction into the reported resolution criterion, rather than fixing the dealiasing kernel to use the exact value
findings.before: `_build_dealias(::TwoThirds,...) = spectral_cutoff(reference, multipliers, T(2 // 3) * (N / 2) * (2π / L))` (rounds the exact `2//3` to `T` first) vs `max_wavenumber` computing `_retained_nyquist_fraction(domain.dealiasing) * (N / 2) * (2π / domain.grid.domain_size[1])` in full (unrounded) precision
findings.after: `_cutoff_wavenumber(strategy, N, L, ::Type{T}) where {T} = T(_retained_nyquist_fraction(strategy)) * T(N / 2) * T(2π / L)`, now called identically by both `_build_dealias` and `max_wavenumber`
findings.why_it_matters: Verified numerically: on a Float32 domain, `T(2//3)` rounds to `0.6666667f0`, slightly above the exact `2/3`, so the dealiasing mask actually built is ~1.3e-6 (relative ~3e-8) wider than the nominal 2/3-Nyquist rule. The chosen fix makes `max_wavenumber` — and hence the grid-mode viscosity solve and the reported `κ_max·η` a run is judged by — agree with that already-too-wide built band, rather than tightening `_build_dealias` to keep the exact fraction and truly enforce the ≤2/3 cutoff the anti-aliasing guarantee depends on. The magnitude is negligible for any physical measurement (Float32-only, ~1e-7 relative) and Float64 domains are unaffected, so this is minor, but it resolves the discrepancy in the direction that keeps the imprecision rather than the direction that would remove it.

findings.title: ConstantPower's amplitude lost its only bound: the removed 1e-12 floor was a ceiling on a division, and the replacement predicate is a sign test
findings.before: amplitude = band_observable > 1e-12 ? forcing.injection_rate / (2 * band_observable) : 0.0
findings.after:
_band_is_empty(band_value) = !(isfinite(band_value) && band_value > zero(band_value))
…
  amplitude = _band_is_empty(band_observable) ? 0.0 :
              forcing.injection_rate / (2 * band_observable)
findings.why_it_matters: The scale-invariance argument written into the new comment ("any constant floor breaks it … Positivity is the whole test") is correct for `BandRescaling`, whose `scale = sqrt(target_band / band_value)` is bounded by an absolute target. It does not transfer to `ConstantPower`, where the floor was not enforcing a scale — it was bounding `injection_rate / (2·band_observable)`, which diverges as band_observable → 0. One shared predicate was applied to two sites with different requirements, and the second site now has no bound at all. The old floor capped the amplitude at 0.1/2e-12 = 5e10; the new predicate caps it at nothing. Witness, run against the head package (8³ Float64 domain, TwoThirds, seeded solenoidal field scaled by 1e-80 — the same flow in different units, which is exactly the case the invariance argument is meant to protect): band_observable = 1.5e-160, HEAD max rate = 3.3333333333333323e158, and the integrating factor exp(A·Δt) at Δt = 1e-3 overflows to Inf on the very first step. BASE returned amplitude = 0.0 and the run continued unforced, which is what the deleted comment ("nothing in the band yet (guard)") promised. Input in [0, 1e-12) was previously refused, so the behaviour-change lane excludes it by construction; nothing else owns it. Float32 reaches the same cliff at band_observable ≈ 1e-38, where T(amplitude) is still finite and `rate .= T(amplitude) .* forcing.indicator` produces Inf inside the band.

findings.title: cfl_timestep's zero-speed fallback was promoted to a universal ceiling, silently halving Δt for every run with u_max < 1
findings.before: return speed > 0 ? sim.cfl * Δx / speed : sim.cfl * Δx
findings.after:
ceiling = sim.cfl * Δx
  return speed > 0 ? min(sim.cfl * Δx / speed, ceiling) : ceiling
findings.why_it_matters: The defect was real (an unforced decaying run running Δt away to ~1e15), but the fix is wider than the defect: it clamps the NORMAL branch, not just the degenerate tail. Because `min(cfl·Δx/speed, cfl·Δx)` picks the ceiling whenever speed < 1, the CFL rule is disabled outright across a whole regime — and speed = 1 is not a physical threshold, it is whatever the code units make it. Witness, run against the head package: a 16³ run at kinetic_energy = 0.02 has u_max = 0.4842635834204808 and cfl = 0.5; HEAD dt = 0.19634954084936207, BASE dt = 0.4054600584716565, ratio = 0.48426358342048087 — exactly u_max. Every such run now takes ~2× the steps to reach the same physical time, with no error and no warning; a clamp fails silently where a throw does not. The default `kinetic_energy = 1.5` gives u_rms = 1.0 and u_max ≈ 2–3, which is why the suite never trips it. Worse, the contract was not updated to match: the function's own surviving comment still reads "The advective-CFL timestep Δt = C·Δx/maxᵢ|uᵢ|", docs/src/notation.md:100 (untouched by this diff) states ``\Delta t = C_{\mathrm{CFL}} \Delta x/\max\lvert\boldsymbol{u}\rvert``, and src/SimulationRun.jl:283 — an error message ADDED by this same diff — asserts "Δt = cfl·Δx/u_max". The change set contradicts itself. A proportionate fix bounds Δt by a physical scale (a turnover time, or an explicit `dt_max` setting), not by the value the rule happens to give at unit speed.

findings.title: The StochasticOU allocation fix removed the host staging that made the device path work, on a GPU-primary package
findings.before: copyto!(field_data(noise_physical), randn(ou.rng, T, size(field_data(noise_physical))...))
findings.after:
# In place: `randn` would allocate a fresh field-scale array on every step of the hot loop, and on
  # a device backend a host array to copy across as well.
  randn!(ou.rng, field_data(noise_physical))
findings.why_it_matters: The comment names the host array as a cost — but on a device backend that host array was the mechanism, not the overhead. `ou.rng` is a `MersenneTwister` (set by the `seed` keyword). Enumerating `methods(Random.randn!)` on Julia 1.12.6 gives only four: two dispatch on `A::Array{Float64}` with a concrete host RNG, one is the no-RNG form, and the fourth is the generic `randn!(rng::AbstractRNG, A::AbstractArray{T})`, which loops `A[i] = randn(rng, T)`. CUDA.jl / AMDGPU only add methods for their OWN device RNGs, so `randn!(::MersenneTwister, ::CuArray)` resolves to that generic loop and hits the scalar-indexing error CUDA.jl throws by default. The base line worked on a device precisely because `randn(rng, T, dims...)` built a host `Array` and `copyto!` performed the transfer. A StochasticOU-forced run that ran on the CUDA backend at base now errors at head — against invariant 4 ("GPU-primary", "no scalar indexing of device arrays"). Nothing in the suite covers it: the diff adds no device test, and StochasticOU is un-exported ("archived … kept tested for the re-add", test/simulation_run.jl:8), so the regression is invisible on CPU. The allocation the fix targets was real; removing the transfer to get it was wider than the defect required.

findings.title: advance! added an unconditional per-step device-to-host readback that the frozen synchronization ledger does not count, and the ledger was not updated
findings.before:
check_deposits(sim.cache)

  sim.clock.time += Δt
findings.after:
check_deposits(sim.cache)
…
  sim.state.scalar_spectral === nothing ||
    isfinite(scalar_variance(sim.state.scalar_spectral)) ||
    error("non-finite scalar at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")
findings.why_it_matters: `scalar_variance(φ̂) = inner(φ̂, φ̂)` is a full field reduction whose result is compared on the host, so it is one blocking device-to-host readback on EVERY step of EVERY scalar-carrying run — not only under a monitoring criterion. test/optimality_audit.jl's `_syncs()` is a hand transcription (its own header lists its sources: `deposit!`, `StationarityCriterion`, `apply_forcing!`, `set_forcing_rate!`, `prepare_forcing!`, `_observe_and_test!`); `advance!` is not among them, and the `scalar variance` entry it does carry belongs to `_observe_and_test!` under `monitor === :skew_scalar`, a different site. Because the instrument is static rather than measured, it cannot notice: every scalar configuration now issues one readback more per step than SYNC_LEDGER records, and the audit passes anyway. CLAUDE.md requires a step-schedule change to update the frozen ledgers "in the same commit, citing the decision"; test/optimality_audit.jl and test/compute_audit.jl are both absent from this diff. This is the ledger-as-oracle trap in its quiet form — not a re-baseline, but a ledger left stale so nothing fails. Separately, the guard throws AFTER `deposit!`, `advect!` and `deposit_sample!` have run and BEFORE `sim.clock` is updated, so the raised `sim` has advanced fields and tracers against an unadvanced clock.

findings.title: fields_modified! silently gained the power to reduce the trajectory integrator's order; its base contract said only that it advances the epoch
findings.before: fields_modified!(cache::ObservablesCache) = (cache.fields_epoch += 1; cache)
findings.after:
fields_modified!(cache::ObservablesCache) =
  (advance_fields_epoch!(cache); cache.history_filled = 0; cache)
findings.why_it_matters: `fields_modified!` is the documented verb for a hand-applied filter, projection or correction. At base it did exactly one thing: bump the epoch, so subsequent reads throw — a loud failure. At head it also zeroes the Lagrangian sample history, which sends an `AdamsBashforth(order = K)` trajectory scheme back into its `EndpointHeun` bootstrap for the next K−1 steps. That is a silent order reduction: no throw, no warning, no observable difference to the caller, just a second-order-in-time trajectory where fourth was requested. The cache and the scheme now share `history_filled` as one mutable counter with two owners, and `restart!(::AdamsBashforth, buffers) = (buffers.cache.history_filled = 0; buffers)` writes the same field, so the history can be reset from three places. The new consequence is documented only in the head docstring ("It also discards the Lagrangian **sample history** this cache carries") — a contract written in the audited window to describe behaviour the same window introduced, which is precisely the shape the audit is told not to take as the standard. The invalidation may well be physically right; the objection is that the only failure mode is a quietly lower-order answer, on a verb whose whole prior design was to fail loudly.

findings.title: MultistepBuffers' documented public fields and the two-argument allocate_buffers were deleted; ObservablesCache gained a fourth type parameter and three positional fields
findings.why_it_matters: `allocate_buffers` is exported (src/GBGIsotropicTurbulence.jl:142, 230) and carries its own API-page entry (docs/src/api/Propagator.md:26), and the base `MultistepBuffers` docstring listed `past`, `steps` and `filled` under `# Fields` — the type-docstring convention's promise that these are reference detail a reader may use. Every previously valid call of the form `allocate_buffers(AdamsBashforth(order = 4), tracers)` is now a MethodError with no deprecation, and every read of `buffers.filled` / `buffers.past` / `buffers.steps` is a field error. `ObservablesCache{PV, PS, TS}` likewise became `ObservablesCache{PV, PS, TS, T}` and its positional constructor gained `particle_velocity_history`, `sample_steps` and `history_filled`, so any hand-written annotation or positional construction breaks too. The package's own oracle for the deleted field was edited in this same window — test/particles.jl went from `@test sim.particle_buffers.filled == 0` to `@test sim.cache.history_filled == 0` — so the suite records only the new shape, and nothing in the change set measures what a caller written against the base API now does. The underlying move (history follows the epoch that invalidates it) is defensible; the point is that it was landed as a silent public-API amputation on a package whose own note says "The API is not frozen; do not build backward-compatibility shims" — which licenses the break but does not make it invisible.

findings.title: The _base_cfl fallback was deleted rather than corrected, turning the documented extension point into a hard error
findings.before:
_base_cfl(::AbstractIntegrator) = 0.3
_base_cfl(::IFRK2) = 0.25
_base_cfl(::IFLowStorageRK3) = 0.5
findings.after:
# NO `::AbstractIntegrator` FALLBACK, matching `allocate_buffers` on the same supertype: a scheme
# that has not declared its stability limit gets a hard error, not a number.
_base_cfl(::IFRK2) = 0.25
_base_cfl(::IFLowStorageRK3) = 0.5
findings.why_it_matters: The stated reason is sound as far as it goes — 0.3 sits above IFRK2's 0.25, so it was never conservative. But the proportionate fix for a fallback that is too loose is to tighten it (0.2, say, below every declared limit), not to remove it. `recommended_cfl` is exported and has its own API-page entry, and it is the default value of `Simulation`'s `cfl` keyword, so any user-defined `AbstractIntegrator` — the abstract type exists precisely to be subtyped — now MethodErrors at `Simulation` construction where it previously ran. That is previously valid usage newly refused; whether the number it used to get was a good one is a separate question from whether deleting it was the minimum change. The justification offered ("matching `allocate_buffers` on the same supertype") is an appeal to the existing arrangement rather than to a first principle, which the package's own self-guard on circular justification flags.

findings.title: A concrete Bool field was widened to Any, and the identity test it enables cannot fail at any call the package makes
findings.before: displaced_velocity_fresh::Bool   # PhaseShift: u_shifted still holds THIS stage's displaced velocity
findings.after: displaced_velocity_source::Any
findings.why_it_matters: Two things happen at once. First, a concrete isbits field in a mutable struct on the hot path became `Any` — a boxed, GC-tracked slot written at every PhaseShift velocity stage, with no validation of what may be stored in it. Second, the new gate `displaced_velocity_current && generator.displaced_velocity_source === û` is not the stronger check it appears to be. The head's own comment concedes the identity half is insufficient ("these containers are written in place, so the same object holds a different stage's velocity a moment later and `===` cannot tell the two apart"), which leaves the real gate as `displaced_velocity_current::Bool = false`, an unverifiable caller assertion. All three in-package call sites — IFLowStorageRK3 once and IFRK2 twice — pass `displaced_velocity_current = true` unconditionally, and each is preceded immediately by `velocity_rhs!` on the very same `û` object, so `source === û` is true by construction at every one of them. The composite condition therefore certifies nothing about the paths the package actually takes; it is the "a bound that cannot fail is not a bound" pattern from decision 37, restated as a freshness check. Its only operative effect is on hand-written callers, where the new `false` default makes them rebuild — a genuine improvement, but achieved by the keyword alone, with the `Any` field and the identity test contributing no protection.

findings.title: The new `fields_modified!(sim)` convenience method throws on the exact call its own docstring describes
findings.before: base had no `fields_modified!` method here at all, and the import line read `using ..Cache: ObservablesCache, check_deposits, particles_modified!, deposit_sample!, velocity_physical, max_speed, particle_velocities`
findings.after: `+fields_modified!(sim::Simulation) = (fields_modified!(sim.cache); sim)` — added under an import line that gained `advance_particles_epoch!` but never gained `fields_modified!`, and only `particles_modified!` was promoted to `import ..Cache:`
findings.why_it_matters: RAN IT. `fields_modified!(sim)` -> `MethodError: no method matching fields_modified!(::Simulation{...})`. Calling `SimulationRun.fields_modified!(sim)` directly also throws, from inside its own body: `MethodError: no method matching fields_modified!(::ObservablesCache{...})`. Without the `import`, line 536 defines a brand-new generic in `SimulationRun` rather than extending `Cache.fields_modified!` — I confirmed `Cache.fields_modified! === SimulationRun.fields_modified!` is `false`, and each carries exactly one method. The umbrella exports Cache's binding, so the method is unreachable from every namespace. Its stated purpose is 'a caller holding a run should not have to know which of the two verbs happens to have the convenience method' — and the verb it adds is the one that does not work. Nothing in test/ calls it, so the 60+ new regression files certify around it.

findings.title: The new CFL ceiling is a statement about velocity units, and it silently changes the physical result of any run whose u_max drops below 1
findings.before: `-  return speed > 0 ? sim.cfl * Δx / speed : sim.cfl * Δx`
findings.after: `+  ceiling = sim.cfl * Δx` / `+  return speed > 0 ? min(sim.cfl * Δx / speed, ceiling) : ceiling`
findings.why_it_matters: MEASURED, BASE vs HEAD, same seed, same 40 adaptive steps of an unforced decaying run at 16^3: BASE reaches t = 16.2507291699 with k = 0.00779794617213; HEAD reaches t = 7.85398163397 with k = 0.0194073748606. HEAD's simulated time is exactly 40 x 0.19635 = 40 x cfl·Δx — the ceiling bound on every one of the 40 steps, so the adaptive rule was switched off for the whole run and Δt became a constant. At the seeded state alone the ratios are: k=0.1 -> head/base = 0.9675; k=0.01 -> head/base = 0.306. The threshold is `max_speed < 1`, which is not a physical condition: rescale the velocity field by 1/10 (a legal rescaling of decaying HIT) and the ceiling starts binding where it did not. The comment's own justification concedes there is no diffusive limit to bound against, then bounds anyway at 'the step this rule gives at unit speed'. The runaway it fixes is real; the fix substitutes a unit-dependent constant for the adaptive rule instead of, say, a turnover- or box-crossing-based cap, and changes computed results for input that was previously valid.

findings.title: `randn!` in place removes the host staging array that is what makes the OU forcing runnable on a device backend
findings.before: `-  copyto!(field_data(noise_physical), randn(ou.rng, T, size(field_data(noise_physical))...))`
findings.after: `+  # In place: `randn` would allocate a fresh field-scale array on every step of the hot loop, and on` / `+  # a device backend a host array to copy across as well.` / `+  randn!(ou.rng, field_data(noise_physical))`
findings.why_it_matters: RAN IT against a stand-in array whose `getindex`/`setindex!` error the way CUDA's `allowscalar(false)` does, with bulk `copyto!` allowed: the HEAD form throws `scalar indexing is disallowed on this array`; the BASE form succeeds. `Random.randn!(::MersenneTwister, ::AbstractArray)` has no bulk path — it is an `eachindex` loop of scalar writes. The comment names the host staging array as the second thing being eliminated, when that array is precisely the mechanism that lets a CPU RNG fill device storage. CLAUDE.md invariant 4 is 'GPU-primary ... no scalar indexing of device arrays', so the allocation this trades away is the cheaper of the two costs. CAVEAT: CUDA is not a dependency of this project, so this is the surrogate, not a CuArray run — but no CPU test in the diff could have distinguished the two forms either, which is the point.

findings.title: The `max_speed` comment's headline allocation number is off by 64x — it is the 64^3 measurement labelled 16^3 — and the timing trade it describes reverses at production grid sizes
findings.before: base had `max_speed(u) = maximum(norm, u)` with no comment and no measurement claim
findings.after: `+# ... that guard costs ~2.9x the plain magnitude and ~1.7x `lpnorm` on this whole-grid reduction — but` / `+# `lpnorm(u, Inf)` ALLOCATES (2 MiB at 16³ here, scaling with the grid) while this route allocates` / `+# nothing. ... Measured both ways rather than argued.`
findings.why_it_matters: RE-RAN ALL THREE NUMBERS. At 16^3: `maximum(norm,u)` 3.1 us / 0 B; `lpnorm(u,Inf)` 2.3 us / 32,888 B; plain magnitude 1.1 us / 0 B. At 64^3: 198.7 us / 0 B, 394.5 us / 2,097,272 B, 72.5 us / 0 B. So (a) '2 MiB at 16³' is the 64^3 figure — 64^3 x 8 B = 2,097,152 exactly; the real 16^3 number is 32 KiB; (b) '~1.7x lpnorm' measures 1.35x at 16^3 and INVERTS at 64^3, where `maximum(norm,u)` is 2x FASTER than lpnorm, so the 'accept the compute cost to avoid the allocation' trade the comment says it deliberated does not exist at any grid a run would use; (c) only '~2.9x the plain magnitude' reproduces (2.8x at 16^3, 2.7x at 64^3). The sentence 'Measured both ways rather than argued' is the load-bearing claim, and it is the one that did not survive re-measurement — no reader lane could have caught this.

findings.title: The documented 2-argument `allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers)` was deleted for AdamsBashforth while its home docstring still advertises it, and the test asserting the old buffer shape was rewritten in the same window
findings.before: `-function allocate_buffers(::AdamsBashforth{K}, tracers::Tracers) where {K}` / `-  past = [similar(tracers.positions) for _ in 1:max(K - 1, 0)]` / `-  return MultistepBuffers(past, zeros(Float64, max(K - 1, 0)), 0, allocate_buffers(EndpointHeun(), tracers))`
findings.after: `+function allocate_buffers(::AdamsBashforth{K}, tracers::Tracers, cache) where {K}` — with `src/Propagator.jl`'s `allocate_buffers` home docstring left verbatim at base, still reading `allocate_buffers(scheme, tracers) -> ParticleIntegratorBuffers`
findings.why_it_matters: RAN THE DOCUMENTED CALL. `allocate_buffers(AdamsBashforth(order=4), tracers)` -> MethodError; the same call for `EndpointHeun` still works, so the generic's one advertised signature now holds for one of its two schemes. `MultistepBuffers` also changed from `mutable` with `past`/`steps`/`filled` to immutable with `cache`/`startup`/`weights`/`nodes`, so any code reading `buffers.filled` breaks — and `test/particles.jl`, the oracle that pinned `sim.particle_buffers.filled == 0/1/3`, was rewritten onto `sim.cache.history_filled` in this same diff. The move of the history into the cache may well be right; the audit point is that the public constructor was withdrawn without its one-concept-one-home docstring being touched, and the only test that would have flagged the shape change was edited to match.

findings.title: A new unconditional per-step full-field reduction and device readback was added to `advance!`, at a site the synchronization ledger does not transcribe — and the ledger was not touched
findings.before: base `advance!` performed no reduction of its own; the blow-up check lived only in `cfl_timestep` as `isfinite(speed)` on the already-cached host number
findings.after: `+  sim.state.scalar_spectral === nothing ||` / `+    isfinite(scalar_variance(sim.state.scalar_spectral)) ||` / `+    error("non-finite scalar at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")` — with the comment conceding `This costs one extra reduction and one readback, and only on a run that carries a scalar.`
findings.why_it_matters: The comment prices the cost and then nothing checks the price. `test/optimality_audit.jl`'s `_syncs` is a hand transcription that names its sources explicitly — `deposit!`, `StationarityCriterion`, `apply_forcing!`, `set_forcing_rate!`, `prepare_forcing!`, `_observe_and_test!` — and `advance!` is not among them; its only 'scalar variance' Sync is gated on `monitor === :skew_scalar`. The row `adaptive dt, stochastic velocity + scalar` still reads `achieved = 3` when the true per-step count for a scalar run is now 4, and `test/optimality_audit.jl` appears nowhere in this diff. I RAN the suite: green. MEASURED the CPU cost as negligible (2.35 us = 0.05% of the step at 32^3; 19.99 us = 0.04% at 64^3) — which is exactly why a CPU test cannot see it: the cost being bounded is the blocking device-to-host sync per step, the eighth audited axis, whose floor is 1. This is the 'unexamined cost' shape CLAUDE.md's own self-guard names.

findings.title: Replacing the 1e-12 band floor with bare positivity changes what the forcing does to previously-valid input, and inverts the NaN path
findings.before: `-  band_value < 1e-12 && return field                   # nothing in the band yet (guard)`
findings.after: `+_band_is_empty(band_value) = !(isfinite(band_value) && band_value > zero(band_value))` and `+  _band_is_empty(band_value) && return field           # nothing in the band yet`
findings.why_it_matters: MEASURED, BASE vs HEAD, on a seeded solenoidal field scaled to band energy 1e-14: BASE `apply_forcing!(BandRescaling(target=1.5, over=:band))` leaves k at 1e-14 (no-op); HEAD rescales it to exactly 1.5 — a 10^14 amplification of a field the old guard classed as empty. The scale-invariance argument for dropping an absolute floor is correct and I do not dispute it; the objection is proportionality. Bare positivity in floating point cannot separate 'the band is physically empty' from 'the band holds cancellation residue', so the fix moved the failure from 'silently unforced' to 'silently amplified by an arbitrary factor', which is the harder failure to notice. Separately the NaN branch reversed direction: BASE (`NaN < 1e-12` is false) propagated NaN through the rescale and poisoned the field visibly; HEAD returns the field untouched, so a blown-up run's forcing now silently no-ops.

findings.title: Removing the `_base_cfl` fallback makes a third-party integrator unable to construct a `Simulation` at all, and the failure names a private helper
findings.before: `-_base_cfl(::AbstractIntegrator) = 0.3`
findings.after: the line is deleted; only `_base_cfl(::IFRK2) = 0.25` and `_base_cfl(::IFLowStorageRK3) = 0.5` remain, under a comment reading `NO ::AbstractIntegrator FALLBACK, matching allocate_buffers on the same supertype`
findings.why_it_matters: RAN IT with a user scheme `struct MyScheme <: AbstractIntegrator end`: `recommended_cfl(MyScheme(), domain)` -> `MethodError: no method matching _base_cfl(::MyScheme)`. Two consequences the comment does not mention. First, `Simulation`'s `cfl` keyword defaults to `recommended_cfl(scheme, domain)`, evaluated before the body runs, so a custom integrator can no longer build a `Simulation` without explicitly passing `cfl` — usage that worked at base now fails at construction. Second, the error surfaces a private, undocumented internal (`_base_cfl`) rather than the public `recommended_cfl` the caller invoked, which is the same class of unhelpful failure that four other edits in this diff were written to eliminate. The reasoning that 0.3 'is not a conservative choice — it sits ABOVE IFRK2's 0.25' is sound; a hard error at a private name is a wider remedy than stating the limit or throwing from `recommended_cfl` itself.

findings.title: StochasticOU's fix for a host allocation replaces it with a device scalar-indexing hazard
findings.before: copyto!(field_data(noise_physical), randn(ou.rng, T, size(field_data(noise_physical))...))
findings.after: randn!(ou.rng, field_data(noise_physical))
findings.why_it_matters: The old line allocated a host Array via randn(ou.rng, T, dims...) and moved it onto the domain's backend array with copyto! — a legitimate bulk host→device transfer that works on CPU, CUDA, and ROCm alike. ou.rng is always a MersenneTwister (a host-only RNG; the `rng::R` field is always constructed as `MersenneTwister(seed)`). Calling `randn!` with a host RNG directly on a CuArray/ROCArray has no GPU-native dispatch to fall back to except Base's generic `randn!(rng, A) = (A[i] = randn(rng, T) for i in eachindex(A))`, which is scalar setindex! on a device array — exactly the invariant CLAUDE.md forbids ("storage is generic AbstractArray … no scalar indexing of device arrays") and something CUDA.jl raises a hard error for by default. The fix correctly removes a genuine per-step host allocation on CPU, but for any run using StochasticOU on the GPU backend this package advertises as primary, prepare_forcing! — called every step from Generator.prepare! — would now fail (or silently degrade to catastrophically slow scalar transfers where allowed) where it previously worked. The only test exercising this path, test/regressions/02-gpu-and-hot-loop-02.jl, is built with `array_type = Array` and checks only @allocated byte counts, so it cannot and does not catch this.

findings.title: advance! grew an unconditional per-step full-field reduction + host readback the frozen sync ledger never priced
findings.before:
sim.clock.time += Δt
  sim.clock.step += 1
  return sim
findings.after:
isfinite(max_speed(sim.cache)) ||
    error("non-finite velocity at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")
  sim.state.scalar_spectral === nothing ||
    isfinite(scalar_variance(sim.state.scalar_spectral)) ||
    error("non-finite scalar at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")

  sim.clock.time += Δt
findings.why_it_matters: The added `max_speed(sim.cache)` check is free — it rereads an already-deposited host scalar. But the comment beside `scalar_variance` admits the cost outright: "This costs one extra reduction and one readback, and only on a run that carries a scalar." scalar_variance(φ̂) computes `inner(φ̂, φ̂)`, a whole-field reduction plus a blocking device-to-host sync, now executed unconditionally on every step of every scalar-carrying run regardless of whether anything downstream needs it that step. test/optimality_audit.jl's SYNC_LEDGER and its `_syncs()` model (which the package's own Verification workflow requires be updated "in the same commit" for any step-schedule/footprint change) list every other per-step host readback by call site — the closing max-speed deposit, StationarityCriterion, each forcing's rate/band observable — but have no entry for this new blow-up-guard reduction, and test/compute_audit.jl is likewise silent on it. The audit exists specifically to make a step-schedule change like this a conscious, recorded decision; here it is an invisible one.

findings.after:

  C_K::Float64
  large_scale::L
  dissipation::D
end
...

_reference(::VonKarmanLarge, ::UnitDissipation) = _VONKARMAN1948

findings.title: scalar_rhs! grew a new keyword whose default silently drops what used to be an automatic optimization for any external caller pairing it with velocity_rhs!
findings.before:
scalar_rhs!(N̂, generator::ResolvedGenerator, û, φ̂, u_consumed, φ, domain::FixedDomain) =
  (_scalar_nonlinear!(domain.dealiasing, N̂, generator, û, φ̂, u_consumed, φ, domain); ...)

end
findings.after:
scalar_rhs!(N̂, generator::ResolvedGenerator, û, φ̂, u_consumed, φ, domain::FixedDomain;
            displaced_velocity_current::Bool = false) =

Now that optimization requires the caller to pass a new keyword whose contract ("only if nothing has changed since velocity_rhs! was called on the same û") is a correctness assertion about call order that a hand-written caller must understand and supply — silently reverting to the slower, always-correct rebuild path if they don't. findings.title: advance!(sim; dt) now rejects dt <= 0 (including dt = 0) where before it silently accepted it

# (no positivity check anywhere in advance!)
findings.after:

findings.title: integral_scale's denominator now excludes the κ = 0 shell, silently changing the computed value for any velocity field carrying a nonzero mean component

weighted = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e / k : zero(e), κ, E))
return oftype(weighted, 3 * π / 4) * weighted / total
findings.after:

findings.title: fields_modified!(sim::Simulation) is a dead shadow method, not the claimed mirror of particles_modified!(sim)
findings.before:
(base 569e6fc has no Simulation method for fields_modified! at all.) The corresponding particles_modified! twin was correctly wired earlier in the same file with `import ..Cache: particles_modified!` plus `using ..Cache: ObservablesCache, check_deposits, deposit_sample!, advance_particles_epoch!, velocity_physical, max_speed, particle_velocities`, followed by `function particles_modified!(sim::Simulation)
  particles_modified!(sim.cache)
  sim.particle_buffers === nothing || restart!(sim.trajectory_scheme, sim.particle_buffers)
  return sim
end`.
findings.after: `fields_modified!(sim::Simulation) = (fields_modified!(sim.cache); sim)` — added right after the particles_modified! method, with NO corresponding `import ..Cache: fields_modified!` (or `using ..Cache: fields_modified!`) anywhere in the file; `fields_modified!` never appears in any using/import line of src/SimulationRun.jl.
findings.why_it_matters: Commit 1eef136 claims: 'fields_modified! never got the Simulation method I gave its particle twin — the same instance-not-class miss the fields/particles split itself came from,' implying the twin was added and now works like particles_modified!(sim). It does not. Because fields_modified! is never imported into SimulationRun's namespace, the definition silently creates a brand-new, unrelated generic function SimulationRun.fields_modified! (Julia only errors 'must be explicitly imported to be extended' when the name was already brought in via using/import — here it wasn't, so no load error, just a disconnected shadow). That local generic has exactly one method, for ::Simulation, so its own body's call fields_modified!(sim.cache) recurses into itself with an ObservablesCache argument and matches nothing. SimulationRun does not export fields_modified!, so the umbrella's public fields_modified! (re-exported only from Cache) still has just the ObservablesCache method. Verified directly by loading the real package: `using GBGIsotropicTurbulence; sim = Simulation(grid_points_per_axis=8); fields_modified!(sim)` throws `MethodError: no method matching fields_modified!(::Simulation{...})`, and `methods(fields_modified!)` lists only the ObservablesCache method. Cache.jl's own docstring for fields_modified! was not updated to advertise a sim form (unlike particles_modified!'s docstring, which explicitly documents both forms and was updated), and no test anywhere in this 605-line diff calls fields_modified!(sim) — only fields_modified!(sim.cache) is ever exercised — so the suite reads green over a claimed fix that produced no working code. This reproduces, inside the very commit that names it, the 'fixing the instance, not the class — and being unable to see it from the inside' failure mode already recorded as a known weakness.

findings.title: StochasticOU's per-step noise fill now scalar-indexes a device array through Base's generic randn! fallback
findings.before: copyto!(field_data(noise_physical), randn(ou.rng, T, size(field_data(noise_physical))...))
findings.after:
# In place: `randn` would allocate a fresh field-scale array on every step of the hot loop, and on
  # a device backend a host array to copy across as well.
  randn!(ou.rng, field_data(noise_physical))
findings.why_it_matters: ou.rng is a MersenneTwister (host-only). Random.randn!(rng::AbstractRNG, A::AbstractArray{T}) — the only method that matches a MersenneTwister against anything other than Array{Float64} — is `for i in eachindex(A); A[i] = randn(rng, T); end` (Random/src/normal.jl:228), i.e. one scalar setindex! per grid point. On a CuArray/ROCArray this either throws GPUArrays' 'scalar indexing is disallowed' error outright, or (if scalar indexing were force-enabled) launches one kernel per element — a total breakage of any GPU/ROCm run using StochasticOU forcing, which is otherwise the package's headline target ('GPU is the primary target'). The commit's own comment even names the device cost of the old copyto! pattern while missing that the old pattern was the only one of the two that actually ran on a device; src/State.jl:109 and :198 still use exactly that copyto!(field_data(...), randn(rng, T, dims...)) pattern for the initial-condition seeders, so the codebase now contains both the safe and the broken form side by side. The one CPU witness that exists for this change (test/regressions/02-gpu-and-hot-loop-02.jl, despite its name) only measures @allocated on array_type = Array and cannot see the scalar-indexing regression at all — it is the textbook CPU-identical/device-broken case this lens exists to catch.

  sim.clock.time += Δt
  sim.clock.step += 1
  return sim
findings.after:

  isfinite(max_speed(sim.cache)) ||
    error("non-finite velocity at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")

The `isfinite(max_speed(...))` half of the same guard is not a new sync (max_speed reads the already-host-resident deposited scalar), but the scalar_variance half is a genuinely new per-step device-to-host crossing the package's own compute/sync instrumentation no longer measures.

findings.title: `viscosity > 0` forecloses the inviscid / truncated-Euler limit, which the solver supported exactly
findings.before:
function FlowConditions(; viscosity, schmidt, velocity_forcing, scalar_forcing)
  # One instance driving both fields conflates their bookkeeping — but only for a strategy that HAS ...   (no numeric check on either argument at 569e6fc)
findings.after:
+  viscosity > 0 ||
+    throw(ArgumentError("`viscosity` must be positive, got $viscosity: it sets the Reynolds number " *
+                        "through Re = 1/ν, and a non-positive value has no dissipation scale"))
findings.why_it_matters: nu = 0 was not a degenerate input: it is only ever MULTIPLIED in this package. `velocity_integrating_factor` returns `coefficient = -generator.conditions.viscosity * τ`, so at nu = 0 the exponential is the identity — the exact, correct integrating factor for the dealiased Euler equation. `dissipation(û, domain, 0)` returns 0, correctly. Nothing divides by nu in the dynamics (verified by grep: the only quotient is nu/Sc, which is finite at nu = 0). Spectrally truncated Euler flow is a standard published DNS study on exactly this kind of dealiased pseudospectral solver, and it is now unreachable through the public API: `Simulation(domain; viscosity = 0.0)` and any hand-built `FlowConditions(; viscosity = 0.0, ...)` both throw. The accompanying comment argues the case for `schmidt` ("Sc = 0 divides by zero and NaNs the scalar on the first step") and then applies the same treatment to `viscosity`, for which no such failure exists — the guard is wider than the defect that motivated it.

findings.title: Deleting the `_base_cfl(::AbstractIntegrator)` fallback closes the documented integrator extension point with no public replacement
findings.before:
-_base_cfl(::AbstractIntegrator) = 0.3
 _base_cfl(::IFRK2) = 0.25
 _base_cfl(::IFLowStorageRK3) = 0.5
findings.after:
+# NO `::AbstractIntegrator` FALLBACK, matching `allocate_buffers` on the same supertype: a scheme
+# that has not declared its stability limit gets a hard error, not a number. ...
 _base_cfl(::IFRK2) = 0.25
 _base_cfl(::IFLowStorageRK3) = 0.5
findings.why_it_matters: `recommended_cfl(scheme, domain)` is the DEFAULT value of `Simulation`'s `cfl` keyword (`cfl::Real = recommended_cfl(scheme, domain)`), so a user-defined `AbstractIntegrator` — an exported, documented supertype whose whole purpose is pluggability — now MethodErrors at run construction rather than getting a working simulation. The only way back is to add a method to `_base_cfl`, which grep shows is unexported, underscore-private, and mentioned in no docstring and no docs page. Previously a third-party scheme worked out of the box and could override `cfl` explicitly if it wanted a different limit. The stated rationale is that 0.3 sits above IFRK2's 0.25 and so is not conservative — an argument for LOWERING the fallback to 0.25, not for deleting it. The comparison drawn to `allocate_buffers` does not hold either: that generic cannot guess a scheme's register set, whereas a conservative CFL number can be and was supplied.

Every hand-assembled run (the workflow the docstrings explicitly cater to: "a hand-assembled run constructs it here") breaks, and the fix is not local: the caller must now build the `ObservablesCache` first with a matching `history_depth`, inverting the construction order. The exported `MultistepBuffers` also lost three public fields in the same edit (`-  const past::Vector{V}` / `-  const steps::Vector{Float64}` / `-  filled::Int`), which test/particles.jl confirms were being read (`-    @test sim.particle_buffers.filled == 0` rewritten to `+    @test sim.cache.history_filled == 0`). The underlying move of the sample history into the cache may well be right; the point is that a documented public arity vanished and the docstring stating it was left behind asserting the opposite.

findings.title: `kinetic_energy > 0` is strict, forecloses the zero-energy seed, and its own error message only justifies non-negativity
findings.before:
function Simulation(domain::FixedDomain;
                    kinetic_energy::Real = 1.5, ...)
  side_length = domain.grid.domain_size[1]
  ε = stationary_dissipation(Li2008(), kinetic_energy, side_length)   (no check at 569e6fc)
findings.after:
+  kinetic_energy > 0 ||
+    throw(ArgumentError("`kinetic_energy` must be positive, got $kinetic_energy: it is " *
+                        "k = ½⟨|u|²⟩, which cannot be negative, and a zero-energy field has no " *
+                        "spectrum to seed"))
findings.why_it_matters: Building a quiescent run and then writing the velocity in by hand — a restart from a stored field, a Taylor-Green or ABC initial condition, a state assembled incrementally — was a working route at base: the seeder's `current_energy > 0 && (field_data(û) .*= sqrt(T(kinetic_energy) / current_energy))` rescaled to a clean zero field, and the caller then wrote `sim.state.velocity_spectral` and announced it. It now throws at the front door, and `scalar_variance >= 0` two lines below shows the asymmetry: the scalar may be seeded at zero, the velocity may not. The message's own justification ("which cannot be negative") supports `>= 0`; only the appended clause reaches for `> 0`. The self-certification is explicit in the oracle: test/regressions/r3-01-numerics-and-types-01.jl carries `# UPDATED 2026-08-21. As written, this reached the NaN by constructing a run with `kinetic_energy = 0.0` — a route a SECOND fix from the same round has since closed at the front door, so the constructor now throws and this block errored rather than passing`, and the test was rewritten from exercising that construction to `@test_throws ArgumentError Simulation(... kinetic_energy = 0.0)`. A test that used the construction as valid was converted into a test that it is forbidden, in the same change set.

findings.title: `integral_scale` silently changed its denominator, so a field with any mean-flow energy now returns a different number than the documented formula gives
findings.before:
-  total = sum(E)
   weighted = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e / k : zero(e), κ, E))
   return oftype(weighted, 3 * π / 4) * weighted / total
findings.after:
+  total = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e : zero(e), κ, E))
   weighted = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e / k : zero(e), κ, E))
+  total > 0 ||
+    throw(ArgumentError("this velocity field carries no energy, so it has no integral scale"))
findings.why_it_matters: Two changes ride in one edit and only the throw is announced. (a) The denominator no longer sums the kappa = 0 shell, so ANY velocity field with a non-zero mean now gets a strictly larger integral scale than it did at base — silently, with no version note, for input that was always valid. The docstring's own display formula, left untouched in this diff, still states the denominator as the full integral over all wavenumbers, and it now disagrees with the code; it also now disagrees with `kinetic_energy`, the package's own spelling of that same integral, which does include the kappa = 0 shell. (b) A pure uniform flow (all energy in the mean) returned 0.0 at base and now throws — the comment concedes exactly this ("let a field whose energy is entirely in the mean flow pass the emptiness guard and return a meaningless zero"), so a previously valid input was converted from a value to an exception without being called out as such. The zero-energy throw alone was the defect; the denominator change is a separate, unflagged numerical decision bundled with it.

findings.title: The new CFL ceiling caps the timestep at a dimensionally arbitrary 'unit speed', silently shrinking Δt for every low-amplitude run
findings.before: -  return speed > 0 ? sim.cfl * Δx / speed : sim.cfl * Δx
findings.after:
+  ceiling = sim.cfl * Δx
+  return speed > 0 ? min(sim.cfl * Δx / speed, ceiling) : ceiling
findings.why_it_matters: `speed` is dimensional (length per time), so `min(cfl*Δx/speed, cfl*Δx)` binds whenever u_max < 1 in code units — that is not a physical scale, it is the numeral 1. The defect being fixed is real (an unforced decaying run with u_max -> 0 runs Δt away to ~1e15), but the fix is far wider than it: a perfectly healthy run seeded at, say, kinetic_energy = 0.015 has u_rms ≈ 0.1 and u_max ≈ 0.3, and its adaptive timestep is now roughly 3x smaller than at base — silently, changing the computed trajectory and the wall-clock cost of every such run, with no diagnostic. The ceiling's own defence ("the step this rule gives at unit speed, which is exactly what the resting case already used") reasons from the pre-existing `speed == 0` branch rather than from any stability or accuracy bound; by the rulebook's own standard that is the existing arrangement supplying its own justification. A bound tied to a physical scale of the run (the box-crossing time, the turnover time, or a caller-supplied `dt_max`) would fix the divergence without touching runs whose speeds happen to be below one.

findings.title: `provenance` now throws for any composed `ModelSpectrum` outside three hard-coded presets, and the documented four-argument constructor was deleted
findings.before:
-    ModelSpectrum(C_K, large_scale, dissipation, ref)
-The plain constructor `ModelSpectrum(C_K, large_scale, dissipation, ref)` takes the four fields
-- `ref` — the `Reference` reported as the model's provenance.
-  ref::Reference
-provenance(m::ModelSpectrum) = m.ref

+provenance(m::ModelSpectrum) = _reference(m.large_scale, m.dissipation)
+_reference(::PopeLargeScale, ::PopeDissipation) = _POPE2000

+                      "model, so it has no reference; the named presets each carry one"))
findings.why_it_matters: The GPU motivation is sound (a `Reference` holds strings, so the struct was not bitstype and a device capture failed), but the remedy removes the user's ability to attribute a composition at all. `ModelSpectrum` is exported and its plain four-field constructor was explicitly documented as callable ("takes the four fields directly, in the order shown"); that call is now a MethodError, and the docstring was rewritten in the same window to describe the three-field form instead. Returning a 'no published source' `Reference` value, or keeping an optional reference outside the device-captured path, would have fixed the bitstype problem without turning a contracted accessor into a thrower.

findings.title: The history-depth check disagrees with itself: `allocate_buffers` accepts a deeper cache that `advect!` then refuses on the first step
findings.before: (neither predicate existed at 569e6fc — MultistepBuffers owned its own `past`/`steps`/`filled`, so no cross-object agreement was possible or required)
findings.after:
src/Particles.jl:389  +  length(cache.particle_velocity_history) >= K - 1 ||
+    throw(ArgumentError("this cache carries ... ; build the cache with `history_depth = $K`"))

src/Particles.jl:469  +  length(past) == K - 1 ||
+    throw(ArgumentError("this `AdamsBashforth(order = $K)` integrates over $(K - 1) past sample(s), " *
+                        "but the buffers it was handed carry $(length(past)) ..."))
findings.why_it_matters: A hand-assembled run that builds `ObservablesCache(domain; particle_velocities = ..., history_depth = 8)` and then `allocate_buffers(AdamsBashforth(order = 4), tracers, cache)` passes the constructor's sufficiency test (7 >= 3) and throws on the very first `advect!` (7 != 3). A construction that its own validator accepted fails at runtime, which is the failure mode the validator was added to prevent. The inconsistency is visible inside the constructor itself: the predicate says `>=` while its error message says "build the cache with `history_depth = $K`", i.e. equality. Either the constructor should demand equality too, or the step-time check should accept a deeper history and read only its first K-1 entries. As written the two guards encode different contracts for the same pairing.

findings.title: cfl_timestep's new ceiling throttles every sub-unit-speed flow, not just the resting/decaying edge case it targets
findings.before:
isfinite(speed) || error("non-finite velocity at step $(sim.clock.step): the run appears to have blown up")
  return speed > 0 ? sim.cfl * Δx / speed : sim.cfl * Δx
findings.after:
ceiling = sim.cfl * Δx
  return speed > 0 ? min(sim.cfl * Δx / speed, ceiling) : ceiling
findings.why_it_matters: The stated defect is real (an unforced flow decaying to speed -> 0 sends the old formula to Δt ~ 1e15). But the fix caps the ADAPTIVE branch at exactly the value the resting branch returns -- i.e. at "unit speed" in whatever units the caller's kinetic_energy picked. For ANY simulation whose characteristic velocity is legitimately below 1 (a smaller kinetic_energy, a decaying run well before it is literally at rest, a different domain_size/units convention), the CFL-adaptive step that used to be sim.cfl*Δx/speed (> ceiling when speed<1) is now silently clamped down to sim.cfl*Δx, throttling the timestep for input that previously worked correctly and was not blowing up. The bound has no physical derivation (not tied to a diffusive or forcing timescale) -- it is just "whatever the resting-branch number happens to be". The new regression test (test/regressions/03-numerics-and-types-03-cfl-zero-speed.jl) only witnesses the exact max_speed==0 case; nothing exercises 0 < speed < 1, so this broader throttling is unverified either way.

findings.title: The empty-band guard for forcing lost its noise margin entirely, trading a real scale-invariance bug for an unaddressed near-zero blow-up risk
findings.before: band_value < 1e-12 && return field                   # nothing in the band yet (guard)
findings.after:
_band_is_empty(band_value) && return field           # nothing in the band yet

_band_is_empty(band_value) = !(isfinite(band_value) && band_value > zero(band_value))
findings.why_it_matters: The stated motivation -- a fixed 1e-12 floor breaks the exact φ->sφ scale symmetry -- is correct, and the diff even records that the team first tried a RELATIVE floor (a whole-field inner(field,field) comparison, per the test/regressions/r4-free-hot-path-02/03.jl comments) and then abandoned it purely for the extra reduction/readback cost, landing on strict positivity with zero margin. That final form has no defense against a band value that is mathematically supposed to be (near-)zero but comes out as a tiny positive float from summation round-off: for BandRescaling this feeds directly into a sqrt(target/band_value) rescale, and for ConstantPower into forcing.injection_rate/(2*band_observable) -- both can produce an enormous amplitude from what used to be safely treated as "empty" under the old 1e-12 floor. No test in the diff exercises a genuinely-near-zero-but-positive band/observable value (only exact zero, negative, or ordinary-magnitude cases), so this new failure mode is not covered by the self-certifying test suite the same commits added.

findings.title: ModelSpectrum's docstring still describes a `ref` constructor parameter that was deleted from the signature and struct

findings.title: StationarityCriterion now aborts run! outright on the very first non-positive dissipation sample, instead of skipping the turnover-clock update and continuing
findings.before: ε > 0 && (criterion.elapsed_turn += Δt * ε / Float64(kinetic_energy(sim.state.velocity_spectral)))
findings.after:
if ε > 0
    criterion.elapsed_turn += Δt * ε / Float64(kinetic_energy(sim.state.velocity_spectral))
  else
    @warn "StationarityCriterion: the dissipation rate is not positive (ε = $ε), so the eddy-turnover clock cannot advance ... stopping."
    return false
  end
findings.why_it_matters: run!'s loop advances the simulation while the callback returns true and stops (without calling advance! again) the moment it returns false. The old code, on a single ε<=0 reading, just skipped the turnover-clock increment and fell through to _observe_and_test! and the max_turnovers check -- it kept the run going (with a real, latent infinite-loop risk if ε stayed non-positive forever). The new code turns ANY single ε<=0 sample -- including a transient one at t=0 before forcing has kicked in, or one from floating-point noise on a nearly-quiescent field -- into an immediate, unconditional halt of the whole warm-up, with no retry and no distinction between 'permanently non-dissipating' and 'not yet dissipating'. Fixing the genuine infinite-loop hazard did not require making the very first sample fatal.

findings.title: max_wavenumber's return type/precision silently changed from always-Float64 to the domain's own element type, changing the computed grid-mode viscosity for Float32 domains
findings.why_it_matters: The stated defect (the built dealias band and the reported cutoff disagreeing on a Float32 grid, because one route rounded the retained fraction to Float32 first) is real and the unification is reasonable. But it is also a quiet contract change: the old expression computed entirely in Float64 regardless of the domain's element type, so max_wavenumber always returned Float64; the new one returns typeof(L), i.e. Float32 for a Float32 domain. SimulationRun.jl's grid-mode viscosity solve (ν = ε^(1/3) * (resolution / max_wavenumber(domain))^(4/3)) now runs at Float32 precision on such a domain where it previously ran at Float64 -- a small but real change to the computed ν (and hence Re_λ) for previously-valid Float32 Simulation() constructions, presented purely as a self-consistency fix with no mention that it also changes the numeric result of grid-mode setup.

findings.title: Simulation's new kinetic_energy > 0 guard fires unconditionally, even in explicit-viscosity mode where a deliberately zero-energy IC might previously have been built
findings.before:
function Simulation(domain::FixedDomain;
                    kinetic_energy::Real = 1.5, κ_max_η = nothing, viscosity = nothing,
                    schmidt::Real = 1.0, ...)
  side_length = domain.grid.domain_size[1]
  ε = stationary_dissipation(Li2008(), kinetic_energy, side_length)
findings.after:
kinetic_energy > 0 ||
    throw(ArgumentError("`kinetic_energy` must be positive, got $kinetic_energy: it is " *
                        "k = ½⟨|u|²⟩, which cannot be negative, and a zero-energy field has no " *
                        "spectrum to seed"))
  ...
  side_length = domain.grid.domain_size[1]
findings.why_it_matters: The guard sits before the viscosity-mode branch and applies identically whether the caller supplies an explicit viscosity or lets the grid solve for one. In grid mode a zero kinetic_energy indeed makes the ν solve degenerate (worth catching). In explicit-viscosity mode, kinetic_energy only feeds the IC seeder, and Simulation(domain; viscosity = ..., kinetic_energy = 0) previously succeeded, producing a genuinely quiescent (zero-velocity) initial state -- a legitimate, if unusual, construction for a scalar-only or fixed-ν test. That path is now refused unconditionally rather than only where the ν-solve actually requires it.

findings.title: The adaptive timestep gained an undocumented ceiling that shrinks Δt for any run whose maximum speed is below 1
findings.before: return speed > 0 ? sim.cfl * Δx / speed : sim.cfl * Δx
findings.after:
ceiling = sim.cfl * Δx
  return speed > 0 ? min(sim.cfl * Δx / speed, ceiling) : ceiling
findings.why_it_matters: The stated defect is a decaying unforced run running away to Δt ≈ 1e15 as u_max → 0. The ceiling chosen bites everywhere u_max < 1, which is nowhere near that pathology, and the cap is dimensionally arbitrary — cfl·Δx is a length, so the crossover sits wherever the user's velocity unit happens to put it. Measured on a live run: Simulation(grid_points_per_axis=16, viscosity=0.05, kinetic_energy=0.05) has max_speed 0.7657, and cfl_timestep drops from 0.25644 to 0.19635, 23% smaller, from the very first step; at u_max = 0.1 it is 10x smaller. Every such run now walks a different trajectory and reports different per-step output, with no error, no warning and nothing in the diff to announce it. The documented contract still says otherwise on four surfaces the diff did not touch — docs/src/notation.md and both ARCHITECTURE copies give `Δt = C_CFL Δx/max|u|`, the comment two lines above the changed code still reads `The advective-CFL timestep Δt = C·Δx/maxᵢ|uᵢ|`, and the new argument-check added in the same commit tells the user `Δt = cfl·Δx/u_max`. The regression witness shipped for this area (test/regressions/03-numerics-and-types-03-cfl-zero-speed.jl) exercises only max_speed == 0, so no oracle covers the 0 < speed < 1 window where the behaviour actually changed.

findings.title: The empty-band forcing guard was replaced by a positivity test, turning a previously inert forcing into a 1e14 amplification
findings.before:
band_value < 1e-12 && return field                   # nothing in the band yet (guard)
  ...
  amplitude = band_observable > 1e-12 ? forcing.injection_rate / (2 * band_observable) : 0.0
findings.after:
_band_is_empty(band_value) && return field           # nothing in the band yet
  ...
  amplitude = _band_is_empty(band_observable) ? 0.0 :
              forcing.injection_rate / (2 * band_observable)
  # with  _band_is_empty(band_value) = !(isfinite(band_value) && band_value > zero(band_value))
findings.why_it_matters: For any band observable in the open window (0, 1e-12] — previously valid input, previously a no-op — the forcing now fires at full strength. Measured: a seeded velocity scaled by 1e-7 (k = 1.5e-14) under the default BandRescaling(target = 1.5, over = :total) is rescaled to k = 1.5 in a single call, an amplification of 1e14 where the base returned the field untouched; the same field under ConstantPower(injection_rate = 0.1) now gets a linear rate of 3.64e12 (base: exactly 0.0), which the integrating factor exponentiates to Inf on the first step. So a quiescent-band run that previously coasted now either jumps or overflows, silently. The scale-invariance argument in the new comment is sound in itself, but the change removes the numerical floor as well as the scale, and the two are separable — a floor relative to the whole-field observable, or simply keeping the run from dividing by 1e-14, would have been the proportionate fix. The added `isfinite` arm changes a second branch in the opposite direction: a NaN band observable now silently skips forcing where it previously propagated the NaN into the field, removing a blow-up signal.

findings.title: Replacing the host-side randn with in-place randn! breaks StochasticOU on the GPU backend, the package's primary target
findings.before: copyto!(field_data(noise_physical), randn(ou.rng, T, size(field_data(noise_physical))...))
findings.after:
# In place: `randn` would allocate a fresh field-scale array on every step of the hot loop, and on
  # a device backend a host array to copy across as well.
  randn!(ou.rng, field_data(noise_physical))
findings.why_it_matters: `ou.rng` is a `MersenneTwister` and `field_data(noise_physical)` is a `CuArray`/`ROCArray` on a device backend. `randn!(::AbstractRNG, ::AbstractArray)` resolves to the generic Random fallback (Random/normal.jl:228) that loops `A[i] = randn(rng, T)` — verified by dispatching it against a setindex!-erroring AbstractArray, which produced the scalar-indexing error. CUDA.jl rejects scalar indexing outright, so this call throws on GPU where the base code (host randn, then copyto! across the bus) worked. That is the exact prohibition in core invariant 4 — 'no scalar indexing of device arrays' — introduced by a change made in the name of invariant 4. The comment's justification even names the device case ('on a device backend a host array to copy across as well') as a cost to remove, when that copy is what made the line work there. The base allocation was a genuine defect, but the proportionate fix is a device-capable RNG, not the generic fallback. Nothing catches it: the suite has no GPU tests, and StochasticOU is un-exported, so this stays latent until the forcing is re-added.

findings.title: advance! gained an unconditional per-step full-field scalar reduction and device readback, while the frozen synchronization ledger that prices readbacks was left untouched
findings.before:
check_deposits(sim.cache)

  sim.clock.time += Δt
findings.after:
check_deposits(sim.cache)

  isfinite(max_speed(sim.cache)) ||
    error("non-finite velocity at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")
  sim.state.scalar_spectral === nothing ||
    isfinite(scalar_variance(sim.state.scalar_spectral)) ||
    error("non-finite scalar at step $(sim.clock.step + 1): the run appears to have blown up")
findings.why_it_matters: Every scalar-carrying run now pays one extra quadratic reduction over the full spectral scalar field plus one blocking device-to-host readback on every iteration — an N³-scale pass added to a hot loop the package declares allocation-free and readback-minimal. test/optimality_audit.jl's SYNC_LEDGER is the instrument that prices exactly this: its `_syncs` list is a hand-written transcription of the per-step readback sites, and it lists 'scalar variance' only under `monitor === :skew_scalar`. The diff adds a site and does not add the row — the scalar row `(adaptive dt, stochastic velocity + scalar) achieved = 3` still reads 3 where the code now issues 4. Because the ledger is a static transcription rather than a measurement, the audit passes unchanged, so the instrument that exists to make a cost change conscious certified a cost change it never saw. CLAUDE.md requires a step-schedule change to update the frozen ledgers in the same commit, citing the decision; neither happened. The guard itself is defensible; making it unconditional and unpriced is the disproportion.

findings.title: step! changed its return value from the (û, φ̂) tuple to state, breaking hand-run loops written against the behaviour that actually shipped
findings.before:
fields_modified!(cache)                     # the step advanced the fields — the cache goes stale
  return û, φ̂                                     [in BOTH IFLowStorageRK3 and IFRK2]
findings.after:
advance_fields_epoch!(cache)                # the step advanced the fields — the cache goes stale
  # `state`, as the single home docstring says and as the in-place convention requires.
  return state
findings.why_it_matters: Both step! methods returned `(û, φ̂)` at the base commit, and the package documents the hand-run loop (`step!` then `deposit!`) as a supported way to drive the solver. Any such loop written against the shipped behaviour — `û, φ̂ = step!(scheme, state, ...)` — now destructures a `ResolvedFields`, which is not iterable, so previously working code fails at the call site. The docstring did say `Returns state.` at base, so the code-vs-docs disagreement was real; but this diff resolves it in the direction that breaks callers rather than the one that does not, and it does so with no deprecation, no mention in the commit subject, and no entry on any user-facing surface. Worth flagging under this lens precisely because the fix is right and the change is still a silent public-contract break.

findings.title: integral_scale changed its denominator and now throws where it previously returned a number
findings.before:
total = sum(E)
  weighted = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e / k : zero(e), κ, E))
  return oftype(weighted, 3 * π / 4) * weighted / total
findings.after:
total = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e : zero(e), κ, E))
  weighted = sum(broadcast((k, e) -> k > 0 ? e / k : zero(e), κ, E))
  total > 0 ||
    throw(ArgumentError("this velocity field carries no energy, so it has no integral scale"))
  return oftype(weighted, 3 * π / 4) * weighted / total
findings.why_it_matters: Two behaviour changes ride together. (a) Any velocity field carrying energy in the κ = 0 shell — a mean flow — now returns a strictly larger L₁₁, by the factor sum(E)/sum_{κ>0}(E), with no announcement. The package's own seeders zero the κ = 0 mode (the envelope has an explicit `ifelse(k2 > zero_value, ...)` guard), so a package-driven run is unaffected — but `integral_scale(û, domain)` is exported and takes any field, and a restarted, externally supplied or hand-built field with a mean flow silently reports a different length scale, which then propagates into flow_parameters, Re_λ and every turnover-based stop criterion. (b) A uniform-flow field previously returned 0.0 (weighted = 0, total > 0) and now throws ArgumentError, so a diagnostic call that used to succeed on valid input now aborts the caller. Only the second is described by the added comment; the denominator change is the one that alters a number, and nothing in the docstring — whose formula still reads as an integral over all κ — was updated to record it.

findings.title: A cluster of element-type re-pinnings changes the numbers every Float32 run produces, and changes a public accessor's return type
findings.before:
_target_factor(field) = field_tensor_order(field) == 0 ? 1.0 : 0.5
[src/State.jl]      current_energy = 0.5 * inner(û, û)
[src/SimulationDomain.jl] spectral_cutoff(reference, multipliers, T(2 // 3) * (N / 2) * (2π / L))
[src/SimulationDomain.jl] return _retained_nyquist_fraction(domain.dealiasing) * (N / 2) * (2π / domain.grid.domain_size[1])
[src/Cache.jl]      max_speed::Float64
findings.after:
_target_factor(field) = field_tensor_order(field) == 0 ? 1 : 1 // 2
[src/State.jl]      current_energy = measure_kinetic_energy(û)
[src/SimulationDomain.jl] _cutoff_wavenumber(strategy, N, L, ::Type{T}) where {T} =
  T(_retained_nyquist_fraction(strategy)) * T(N / 2) * T(2π / L)
[src/SimulationDomain.jl] return _cutoff_wavenumber(domain.dealiasing, N, L, typeof(L))
[src/Cache.jl]      max_speed::T
findings.why_it_matters: Each edit is individually defensible and each changes a Float32 run's output. `0.5 * Float32` promotes to Float64 while `(1//2) * Float32` stays Float32 (verified), so BandRescaling's band and total observables — and therefore the rescale factor `sqrt(target_band/band_value)` applied to the field — are now computed at Float32 precision every step, a ~1e-7 perturbation that compounds over a run. The seeder's `0.5*inner(û,û)` -> `inner(û,û)/2` does the same to the initial-condition rescale, so a Float32 run starts from a different field. `_cutoff_wavenumber` rounds the retained fraction and both factors to Float32 before multiplying: measured at N = 64, L = 2π(f32), the built dealias cutoff moves by 2.8e-8 relative and `max_wavenumber` by 5.8e-8 relative and from Float64 to Float32, which shifts the grid-mode viscosity by 1.5e-7 relative (0.04258876547 -> 0.04258875921) and can flip membership for a mode sitting on the band boundary. Separately, `ObservablesCache` gained a fourth type parameter, so any `ObservablesCache{PV,PS,TS}` annotation stops matching, and `max_speed(cache)` now hands a Float32 run a Float32 where it handed a Float64. No Float32 regression witness exists in the 100-odd files added, so nothing in the change set measures the drift it introduces.
